active_themes.label: Gulf Oil Slowly Returns
active_themes.summary: Brent fell 5.85% to $92.57 and WTI fell 4.38% to $86.85, the lowest in this stretch, as tanker traffic through Hormuz improved, with liquefied natural gas shipments there at their highest since the war began. Oil is now trading on the flow of ships rather than on the incidents. The open question is whether Brent holds below $95 if another shipping incident occurs.

active_themes.label: AI Spending Backlash
active_themes.summary: The Nasdaq rose 2.74% to 25,253, reclaiming 25,000 after Thursday's 5.52% rout. Two rebound sessions have repaired only part of that loss. The Russell 2000 gained more than the Nasdaq today, so the bounce was driven by oil and rate relief across the market rather than a fresh vote of confidence in AI spending. The open question is whether 25,000 holds on a down day, with 24,000 as the line that would signal repricing.

active_themes.label: Fed Eyes Another Hike
active_themes.summary: The dollar fell 0.64% to 101.65, giving back most of last week's jump after strong payrolls, as cheaper oil softened the case for a December hike. Inflation at 3.7% still keeps the Fed leaning toward gradual hikes. The next inflation report is the test of whether the hike case is fading or just paused.

active_themes.label: Global Borrowing Costs Climb
active_themes.summary: The 10-year yield held at 4.86% and the 30-year at 5.26% despite the oil drop and the stock rally. Bonds are not yet pricing the inflation relief that stocks are. The open question is whether the inflation report lets the 10-year slide toward 4.75% or pushes it back toward 5.00%.

active_themes.label: Democratic Sweep Reaction
active_themes.summary: The Democratic sweep first read as relief, then as a regulatory threat to AI. Today's tech bounce suggests part of that fear was overdone, but nothing in policy has changed. The open question is whether tech's losses outweigh the relief elsewhere, and a Senate Banking Committee led by Elizabeth Warren from January adds a new regulatory pressure point for financial firms.

active_themes.label: Iran War Resumption Risk
active_themes.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard says two tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, and oil still fell sharply. Markets are treating the diplomatic and political track as stronger than the incidents. The open question is whether these fires become a pattern of sustained attacks on shipping, which would erase today's oil drop.

open_watchlist.meaning: Small caps are carrying the market's leadership as yields ease, so the rotation out of mega-cap tech is lasting rather than a one-day move.
Bond buyers finally believe cheaper oil will last, which would be the first real sign of relief on borrowing costs.
The longest borrowing costs would be pushing meaningfully higher, deepening the strain on mortgages, stocks and company borrowing.
Bond buyers are ignoring cheaper oil and today's yield relief has failed.
Renewed inflation pressure makes a Fed hike more likely and removes the one cushion stocks could still lean on.
That would take out Thursday's low area and signal investors are repricing AI stocks rather than just panicking, so today's bounce was a pause.
That would mean hike pricing is intensifying beyond today's reaction, adding pressure on gold, overseas earnings and risk assets.
Oil would be pricing real normalization in Hormuz shipping, which strengthens the case that the inflation threat is fading.
Today's calm would have been temporary and the fear from the tech rout would be returning.

open_watchlist.condition: The S&P 500 closes below 7,375, erasing all of today's gain.
open_watchlist.meaning: Today's rally would be shown to have been a one-day bounce rather than the start of a recovery.
